Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verses 1–3:

﴿Created man﴾.

This is a second report (khabar thani), and what is meant by "man" (al-insan) is the genus of mankind. This is a preparation (tamhid) for the report that follows, which is ﴿He taught him eloquent speech (al-bayan)﴾ [al-Rahman: 4].

This is a matter they do not dispute. However, since they turned away from its requirement, which is singling out God Most High in worship (ifrad Allah ta'ala bil-'ibadah), the report about it was delivered to them in the style of enumeration without conjunction, like one who lists for the addressee the occasions of his errors and heedlessness. This is a second rebuke (tabkit thani).

In the creation of man there are two indications. The first is the indication that God Most High alone is divine (tafarrud Allah ta'ala bil-ilahiyyah). The second is the indication of God's blessing upon man.

Creation is a great blessing, because in it there is an honouring of the created being by bringing it out from the depths of non-existence (ghayahib al-'adam) into the place of manifestation of existence in concrete entities. He placed the creation of man before the creation of the heavens and the earth because of what you have just come to know of the relation of its being followed by the teaching of the Qur'an.

The predicate coming as a verb after the subject (musnad fi'lan ba'da al-musnad ilayhi) indicates the strengthening of the judgment (taqawwi al-hukm). You may also take it to be for restriction (al-takhsis), by treating them as one who denies that God created man, because they worshipped other than Him.

﴿He taught him clear expression (al-bayan)﴾ is a third statement. It contains a reminder of the blessing of making one's meaning clear and a favour bestowed by that blessing, after the favour of creation. That is, He taught mankind to express what is in their minds so that others benefit from them and they benefit from others.

Al-bayan (clear expression) is the disclosure, through speech, of the intentions and aims that lie in the heart. It is by this that man is distinguished from the rest of the animal kinds, so it is among the greatest of blessings.

As for expression without speech, such as signs, gestures and the glance of the eye, it too is among the distinguishing qualities of man, although it falls short of expression by speech.

The meaning of God's teaching man al-bayan is that He created in him the capacity to know this and inspired him to establish language for mutual understanding. This was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31] in Surat al-Baqarah.

In this there is an indication that the blessing of expression is the most exalted of the blessings upon man. He listed the blessing of the religious obligations, and in this there is an honouring of the additional sciences concerning human expression, namely the distinctive features of language and its refinements.

The predicate coming as a verb after the subject serves to convey the strengthening of the judgment.

In this there is also the rebuke you have just come to know. Its basis is that they did not thank Him for the blessing of expression, since they spent a large part of their speech on what distracts them from devoting worship to God alone, and on what they dispute with those who call them to guidance.

﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning.﴾

This is a fourth predicate (khabar) about the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). Otherwise its mention here would be without connection, and it would become a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh). The link (rabit) between the clause and the subject is an implied pronoun: "by His reckoning," meaning the reckoning and regulation of the Most Merciful.

This is an argument for the exclusive creation of the star of the sun and the sphere of the moon, and a favour (imtinan) by what He placed in them of benefits for people. It also refers to the order of their movement, through which the arrangement of people's dealings is made precise, and through which they prepare for what they need when their climates and livelihoods change. The favour includes the benefits they gain from this. That this statement follows the style of enumeration, along with what you have already learned of rebuke (tabkit), has the following aspect: they were heedless of the wisdom in the order of the sun and the moon, and of what that order indicates about God's sole determination of it. So some of them occupied themselves with worshipping the sun and others with worshipping the moon, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to God, who created them, if it is Him that you worship.﴾ [Fussilat: 37].

This clause was given in nominal form (ismiyya) to emphasise its magnitude by beginning with the names of the sun and the moon, and to indicate that their reckoning is fixed and does not change since the beginning of creation, which announces the wisdom of the Creator. By making the names of the sun and the moon the subject of the predicate, it dispensed with splitting the predicate into two predicates, one indicating the argument and the other indicating the favour, as occurs in His saying: ﴿He created man﴾ [al-Rahman: 3] ﴿He taught him the expression﴾ [al-Rahman: 4].

Al-husban (reckoning) is the verbal noun of hasiba, meaning "counted," like al-ghufran (forgiveness).

The ba' (bi-) indicates association (mulaabasa) and is a stationary adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqirr) that is the predicate concerning the sun and the moon. The implied meaning is: "both are existing by a reckoning," that is, in association with a reckoning, meaning for the calculation of people of their positions of movement.

Attributing this association to the sun and the moon is a figurative attribution of the rational kind (majaz 'aqli), because the sun and the moon are the cause of people's involvement with their reckoning. As you say, "You are under my care," where you make your care associated with the addressee in a notional association. Compare His saying: ﴿Indeed you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48]. This was already mentioned in His saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾ [al-An'am: 96] in Surat al-An'am. Al-husban is a metonymy (kinaya) for the regularity of their movement in a consistent manner, such that people's reckoning of it and their timing by it is not disrupted.

The mention is restricted to the sun and the moon, not the rest of the stars, even though there is in the others a reckoning of the seasons (anwa'), of heat and cold, such as al-Jawza', al-Shi'ra, the mansion of al-Asad, and al-Thurayya. This is because these two stars are the most apparent to all people, and understanding their conditions does not require teaching of timing as the other stars do.

Also, because this surah is built on the mention of paired things, and the sun and the moon are a pair in the common knowledge of people: the sun is a heavenly star, because it is higher than the earth, and the earth revolves around it and is within the solar system. The moon is an earthly star, because it is lower than the earth and follows it, like the rest of the moons of the planets. So the mention of the sun and the moon is like the mention of the heaven and the earth, the East and the West, and the two seas.

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿The sun and the moon [follow] a reckoning﴾ [Ar-Rahman 55:5]. He coordinated the report with the report for the reason already mentioned: the prostration of the sun and the moon is to Allah, the Exalted, and this is a transition from enumerating the benefits in the heavens to enumerating the benefits in the earth. He made the word "al-najm" (the star, or low-growing plant) the link of the transition because it is suitable for both: it may mean the stars of the sky, and it may also mean what is called a najm among the plants of the earth, as will come.

The clause ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ was coordinated and not separated. It therefore moved from the style of listing reports to the style of coordinating some reports with others, because the reports that follow the coordinating particles are not intended as a list, since there is in them no implied rebuke of the polytheists. The report of the prostration of the star and the tree is intended to awaken the listener to what this indicates of the greatness of power, through a symbolic indication (dalālah ramziyyah). Moreover, since the context required gathering similar pairs after mentioning the sun and the moon, this called for the method of connection by coordination, on the basis of the common element of opposition.

The clause was made to begin with the subject (al-musnad ilayh) so that it would take the form of the opening of the clause to which it is coordinated. The predicate was expressed as a present-tense verb to indicate the renewal and recurrence of this prostration, in line with the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows [too] in the mornings and the evenings﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 13:15].

The word "al-najm" is used as a collective noun (ism jam') for the stars of the sky. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [An-Najm 53:1]. It is also used in the singular, and its plural is "nujūm." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿and the retreat of the stars﴾ [At-Tur 52:49]. It was transmitted from Mujahid that its meaning here is the stars of the sky.

The word "al-najm" is also used for plants and herbage that have no stalk, so that they lie close to the ground. It was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that the star in this verse means the plant that has no stalk. "Al-shajar" means the plant that has a stalk and rises above the surface of the earth. Humans and animals benefit from both.

Thus there result from the words ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾, after the words ﴿The sun and the moon [follow] a reckoning﴾ [Ar-Rahman 55:5], two parallel pairs in motion and stillness. This is among the complete rhetorical embellishments (al-muḥassināt al-badīʿiyyah).

"Al-sujūd" is used for placing the face on the ground with the intention of glorification. The verb "waqaʿa" (to fall) on the ground is also used figuratively, either as a metonymy by association of generality (mursal, ʿalāqat al-iṭlāq) or as a metaphor (istiʿārah). From this comes the expression "a palm tree that is prostrate" (nakhlah sājidah), when its fruit bends it down. Thus the prostration of the stars of the sky is their descent toward the directions of their setting; the prostration of the plant of the earth is its clinging to the dust like one who prostrates; and the prostration of the tree is its bending when the winds blow and its branches drawing close to those who pick its fruit and those who beat its leaves. So the verb "yasjudān" is used in two figurative senses: approaching the one who reaches for it, and indicating the greatness of Allah, the Exalted, by likening the shadows of these two cast upon the earth to prostration, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows [too] in the mornings and the evenings﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 13:15] in Surat al-Ra'd, and as Imru' al-Qais said:

*He topples them onto their chins, the trees of the kanhabal.*

He said "on their chins" so that the bending down (al-inkibāb) would be likened to a person falling upon the ground with his face. Therefore there is here an implicit metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah), and mentioning the chins is an imaginative evocation (takhyīl). On this basis the verb "yasjudān" here is used in its figurative sense. This indicates that Allah created in the existing things many indications that He is their Originator and Subjugator. In all of them there are rational indications (dalālāt ʿaqliyyah), and in some or most of them there are other symbolic and imaginative indications, so that minds that differ in their capacity for reasoning may benefit from them.

﴿And the heaven He raised high, and He set up the balance.﴾ ﴿That you not transgress in the balance.﴾ ﴿And establish the weighing with justice, and do not make the balance deficient.﴾

In this verse the rhetorical device of antithesis (muqabalah) continues, pairing things that resemble opposites. Having paired the mention of the sun and the moon with the mention of the star and the tree, the verse now mentions the creation of the heaven and the creation of the earth.

The discourse returns to the mode of predicating a verbal predicate of the subject, as in His saying ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ [al-Rahman: 1] ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Rahman: 2]. This clause is coordinated with the preceding statement, so it has the same meaning.

Raising the heaven implies its creation. Its raising is mentioned because it is the locus of reflection on the wondrous creation. The meaning of "He raised it" is that He created it raised up without pillars, just as one says to a tailor, "Widen the collar of the shirt," meaning, "Sew it wide." Moreover, mere elevation indicates the loftiness of its station and its nobility, because in it is the origin of God's decrees and the source of His command, and because it is the place of the angels. This is the use of a word in both its literal and its figurative sense.

Placing "the heaven" before the verb that governs it adds emphasis to the call to reflect on its creation.

Al-mizan (the balance): its original sense is the name of the instrument of weighing. Al-wazn (weighing) is the determination of the equivalence of things and the precise measurement of their weights, and it is a pattern (mif'al) derived from the root w-z-n. It was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿And the weighing that Day is the truth; so whoever's scales are heavy﴾ [al-A'raf: 8] in Surat al-A'raf. The term al-mizan became widely used for justice through the metaphor of applying the word "balance" to justice, by way of likening the intelligible to the perceptible.

Here al-mizan is meant as justice, like the sense in His saying ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], because it is what God set down, that is, what He appointed to establish the order of creation. So "setting" (wad') here is used metaphorically for "making/appointing," and it is like "sending down" in His saying ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the balance﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. From this is the saying of Abu Talhah al-Ansari: "Indeed, the dearest of my properties to me is the well of Ha', and indeed it is a charity to God, so place it, O Messenger of God, wherever God shows you," that is, appoint it and designate it for what God directs you to.

Thus the use of "setting" (wad') in the verse, after the mention of the raising of the heaven, is a contrastive correspondence (mushakalah didiyyah), and it gives the appearance of antithesis with His saying "He raised it." So there are two rhetorical embellishments (muhsinan badi'iyyan) in it.

He joined this with the raising of the heaven to honour the matter of justice, by attributing it to the higher world, which is the world of truth and virtues, and by stating that it descended to the earth from the heaven, that is, it is among what God commanded. For this reason the mention of justice recurs together with the mention of the creation of the heaven, as in His saying ﴿He it is who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stages, that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. God did not create that except in truth﴾ [Yunus: 5] in Surat Yunus; and His saying ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth﴾ [al-Hijr: 85] in Surat al-Hijr; and His saying ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38] ﴿We did not create them except in truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39] in Surat al-Dukhan. This confirms the transmitted saying: "By justice the heavens and the earth stand." Since the command to establish justice was among the most important things God enjoined upon His Messenger ﷺ, the mention of his appointment of it was joined with the mention of the creation of the heaven, as if it were said: "and in it He set the balance."

The particle "an" (that) in His saying ﴿an la tatghaw﴾ (that you not transgress) may be interpretive (tafsiriyyah), because the verb "He set the balance" carries in it the sense of commanding people to justice. The command contains the sense of speech without its letters, so it is apt that its explanation be introduced by the interpretive particle "an." Thus the prohibition against wasting justice in most transactions is an explanation of this. In that case "la" is prohibitive (nahiyah).

It may also be that "an" is verbal-source (masdariyyah), with a genitive particle, lam al-jarr, omitted before it. The estimate is: "so that you do not transgress in the balance." Under both possibilities, "the balance" means what includes justice and includes that by which things are measured and the like in buying and selling. That is, among the benefits of sending down the command to justice is that you avoid transgression in establishing the weighing in dealings. In that case "la" is negating, and the verb ﴿tatghaw﴾ is in the subjunctive governed by the verbal-source "an."

The word "balance" permits both meanings, in the manner of using a homonym (mushtarak) in both of its senses. In the word "balance" and what accompanies it, namely the verb "set" (wada'a), the two verbs "do not transgress" (la tatghaw) and "establish" (aqimu), the preposition "bi" in "bil-qist," the preposition "fi" in "fi al-mizan," and the word "qist," all these converge to convey these meanings, and this is part of the inimitability of the Qur'an.

Transgression (al-tughyan) is the rejection of truth deliberately and with contempt for its adherents. So the meaning of transgression in justice is making light of its neglect and weakness in restraining oneself from injustice. The meaning of transgression in weighing measurable quantities is cheating in them (tatfif).

The "fi" in His saying "fi al-mizan" is a figurative locative, meaning that the prohibition concerns even the least transgression in the balance. That is, the prohibition is not against wasting the whole balance, but against every transgression connected to it in the manner of a locative. Like this is His saying ﴿and provide for them from it and clothe them﴾ [al-Nisa': 5], meaning "provide for them from some of it." And like the saying of Sabrah ibn 'Amr al-Faqa'si:

Sabrah ibn 'Amr al-Fa'qasi, and we drink from their prices and we gamble.

Here he meant that they drink wine with some of the prices of their camels and gamble, that is, that they have other benefits from them, namely giving and eating from them, as in his saying at the beginning of the verse:

We favour with them our equals and we humiliate them.

His saying ﴿And establish the weighing with justice﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ under the possibility that the coordinated clause is interpretive, and with the clause ﴿and He set the balance﴾ under the possibility that the clause it is coordinated with is causal (ta'lil).

Iqamah (establishing) is making a thing upright, and it is a figure for bringing it about in the most complete manner that is intended for it. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿and who establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-wazn (weighing), in its true reality, is the realization of the equivalence of bodies in weight, and here it is meant to include the measurement of quantities, which is measuring by volume and by standard.

Al-qist (justice) means justice. It is an arabicised word from Greek (Rumiyyah), and its original form is qistas, which was then abbreviated in Arabic, so they said at one time "qistas" and at another "qist." It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿and We set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Anbiya': 47] in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The "bi" (with) is for accompaniment.

The meaning is: make justice accompany whatever you evaluate among your affairs, as He said ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾ [al-An'am: 152], and as He said ﴿Let not the hatred of a people prompt you to not be just﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]. So His saying "bil-qist" is a stationary adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), or the "bi" is causal (sababiyyah), meaning: observe in establishing the estimation what justice requires. In that case "bil-qist" is a free adverbial (zarf laghw) attached to the verb.

The polytheists used to be accustomed to cheating in weighing, as came in His saying ﴿Woe to those who give less [than due], who, when they take a measure from people, take in full, but when they give by measure or weight to them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1–3]. Since cheating was one of the customs of the polytheists, the verse was directed to draw attention to it. On both considerations the explanation of His saying ﴿and do not make the balance deficient﴾ is also derived. If "the balance" in it is understood to mean justice, the meaning is a prohibition against negligence about justice through carelessness or laxity, after the prohibition against transgression in it. The explicit mention of the word "balance" in place of a pronoun would then be a reminder of God's great care for justice. If it is understood to mean the instrument of weighing, the meaning is a prohibition against defrauding people in the weighing done for them, as He said in Surat al-Mutaffifin ﴿and when they measure or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 3].

Ikhsar (causing loss) means making another party a loser, and khasarah (loss) means deficiency.

So on the reading of "the balance" as justice, ikhsar means making the rightful party a loser and defrauded; "the balance" is then in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. On the reading of "the balance" as the instrument of weighing, ikhsar means deficiency, that is, do not make the balance deficient, as He said ﴿And do not diminish the measure and the balance﴾ [Hud: 84]. You have come to know this wondrous arrangement in the verse, which is suited to these different interpretations.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verse 10–12:

Page 241
﴿And the earth He laid down for the creatures.﴾ ﴿Therein is fruit, and palm trees with sheaths.﴾ ﴿And grain with its husk, and fragrant plants.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿And the sky He raised up﴾ [al-Rahman: 7], and it is its counterpart in pairing: "laying down" (waḍʿ) corresponds to "raising up" (rafʿ), and thus the rhetorical device of antithesis (ṭibāq) is achieved twice. The meaning of "He laid it down" (waḍaʿahā) is that He lowered it for them, i.e., He made it beneath their feet and sides, to enable them to benefit from it with all the benefits and treatments they have from it.

The lām in "for the creatures" (lil-anām) indicates purpose (lil-ajal). As for "al-anām" (the creatures), the views of the lexicographers and exegetes differ concerning it. Al-Jawhari did not mention it, nor did al-Raghib in his Mufradat al-Qur'an, nor Ibn al-Athir in al-Nihaya, nor Abu al-Baqa' al-Kafawi in al-Kulliyyat. Al-Zamakhshari explained it by saying: "the creation, which is everything that appears on the surface of the earth of living creatures having a soul." This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and a group of the Successors (tabiʿun). And also from Ibn ʿAbbas: that it refers to humankind alone. It is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) with no singular form from its own root.

The context of the verse favours that what is meant by it is humankind, because it is in the setting of bestowing favour and attention to mankind, like His saying: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29].

Apparently it is a non-derived noun, and it has dialectal forms: anām like saḥāb, anām like sabāṭ, and unīm like amīr.

The clause ﴿Therein is fruit﴾ to the end of it explains the clause ﴿And the earth He laid down for the creatures﴾. The fronting of "therein" (fīhā) before the subject is for the sake of emphasis on what the earth contains.

Since His saying ﴿He laid it down for the creatures﴾ includes a laying down and a reason for that laying down, the clause explaining it contains what carries lesson and favour.

Al-fākihah (fruit) is a name for what is eaten for enjoyment (tafakkuh), not as sustenance; it is derived from fakiha, like fariha, when one's soul is pleased by conversation and laughter. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So you would be left amazed (tatafakkahūn)﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 65], because eating what is pleasant to the palate, and is not necessary for it, occurs only in a state of relaxation.

Page 242
Al-fākihah is like fruits and vegetables, from almonds, walnuts and pistachios.

He conjoined the palm tree to the fruit. It is the date-palm tree, and it is the most important fruit-bearing tree for the Arabs among whom the Qur'an was revealed. It yields varieties of fruit: fresh dates (rutab), half-ripe dates (busr), and dried dates (tamr), and it is both fruit and staple food.

The description of the palm tree as ﴿with sheaths (dhāt al-akmām)﴾ is a descriptive epithet for embellishment. It is thus a consideration of the stages of the palm's fruit, and a reminder of favour through its beauty and loveliness, like His saying: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]. So He bestowed favour through their benefits and the goodliness of their appearance.

Al-akmām is the plural of kumm (with a kasra on the kāf), which is the sheath of the palm's fruit, and it is called al-kufurrā. The sheaths are not something from which benefit is derived, so it is determined that mentioning them with the palm is for embellishment.

﴿And grain with its husk (al-ḥabb dhū al-ʿaṣf)﴾: this is the grain whose plant has ears (sanābil), and has leaves and stalks, which becomes straw (tibn). That leaf and stalk is al-ʿaṣf, i.e., what the winds sway (taʿṣifuhu al-riyāh). This is a description of barley and wheat, on which the sustenance of most people depends, and likewise what resembles them, such as salt-grain (salt) and rice.

Al-ʿaṣf was so named because the winds sway it, i.e., move it. He described the grain as ﴿with its husk﴾ for embellishment and to remind of the favour of the beauty of the crop when it appears in its ear in its fields, parallel to the description of the palm as "with sheaths", and because in the thing described and its description are the sustenance of humankind and their animals.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿And grain with its husk and fragrant plants﴾ with al-ḥabb in the nominative, al-rayḥān in the nominative, and dhū in the nominative. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read al-ḥabb and dhū in the nominative and al-rayḥān in the genitive, as a conjunction with al-ʿaṣf. Ibn ʿAmir read all three nouns in the accusative, and the sign of the accusative in (dhā al-ʿaṣf) is the alif. Likewise it is written in the Syrian codex, as a conjunction with "the earth," or it is in the sense of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ).

Al-rayḥān: what has a pleasant fragrance from flowers and herbs. It is on the pattern fa'lān from al-rā'iḥah (scent), and it is only named after that which has a good fragrance. This is a consideration and a reminder of favour through the plants in which fragrances are deposited, such as the rose, jasmine, and what is called green basil.

The clause ﴿Therein is fruit﴾ to the end of it explains the clause ﴿And the earth He laid down for the creatures﴾. The fronting of "therein" (fīhā) before the subject is for the sake of emphasis on what the earth contains.

Since His saying ﴿He laid it down for the creatures﴾ includes a laying down and a reason for that laying down, the clause explaining it contains what carries lesson and favour.

Al-fākihah (fruit) is a name for what is eaten for enjoyment (tafakkuh), not as sustenance; it is derived from fakiha, like fariha, when one's soul is pleased by conversation and laughter. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So you would be left amazed (tatafakkahūn)﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 65], because eating what is pleasant to the palate, and is not necessary for it, occurs only in a state of relaxation.

Al-fākihah is like fruits and vegetables, from almonds, walnuts and pistachios.

He conjoined the palm tree to the fruit. It is the date-palm tree, and it is the most important fruit-bearing tree for the Arabs among whom the Qur'an was revealed. It yields varieties of fruit: fresh dates (rutab), half-ripe dates (busr), and dried dates (tamr), and it is both fruit and staple food.

The description of the palm tree as ﴿with sheaths (dhāt al-akmām)﴾ is a descriptive epithet for embellishment. It is thus a consideration of the stages of the palm's fruit, and a reminder of favour through its beauty and loveliness, like His saying: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]. So He bestowed favour through their benefits and the goodliness of their appearance.

Al-akmām is the plural of kumm (with a kasra on the kāf), which is the sheath of the palm's fruit, and it is called al-kufurrā. The sheaths are not something from which benefit is derived, so it is determined that mentioning them with the palm is for embellishment.

﴿And grain with its husk (al-ḥabb dhū al-ʿaṣf)﴾: this is the grain whose plant has ears (sanābil), and has leaves and stalks, which becomes straw (tibn). That leaf and stalk is al-ʿaṣf, i.e., what the winds sway (taʿṣifuhu al-riyāh). This is a description of barley and wheat, on which the sustenance of most people depends, and likewise what resembles them, such as salt-grain (salt) and rice.

Al-ʿaṣf was so named because the winds sway it, i.e., move it. He described the grain as ﴿with its husk﴾ for embellishment and to remind of the favour of the beauty of the crop when it appears in its ear in its fields, parallel to the description of the palm as "with sheaths", and because in the thing described and its description are the sustenance of humankind and their animals.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿And grain with its husk and fragrant plants﴾ with al-ḥabb in the nominative, al-rayḥān in the nominative, and dhū in the nominative. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read al-ḥabb and dhū in the nominative and al-rayḥān in the genitive, as a conjunction with al-ʿaṣf. Ibn ʿAmir read all three nouns in the accusative, and the sign of the accusative in (dhā al-ʿaṣf) is the alif. Likewise it is written in the Syrian codex, as a conjunction with "the earth," or it is in the sense of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ).

Al-rayḥān: what has a pleasant fragrance from flowers and herbs. It is on the pattern fa'lān from al-rā'iḥah (scent), and it is only named after that which has a good fragrance. This is a consideration and a reminder of favour through the plants in which fragrances are deposited, such as the rose, jasmine, and what is called green basil.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾.

The *fa'* (ف) here is for *tafri'* (تفريع, deduction or consequence) from the blessings already mentioned, which are interwoven with the evidences of the Messenger's truthfulness (ﷺ) and of the Qur'an's divine origin. The evidences of God's greatness and wisdom are presented in the form of a question about specifying a particular blessing of God's blessings, whose denial is impossible for them. This verse is a *tadhyil* (تذييل, a concluding appendix) to what precedes it.

*Ayyi* (أيّ) is an interrogative asking to specify one member of the category to which it is attached. Here it is used for *taqrir* (تقرير, affirmation) by mentioning the opposite of what would bring it close, like His saying ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ (Al-Sharh: 1). I explained this at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ (Al-An'am: 130) in Surat al-An'am. That is, none of you can deny the blessings of God.

*Al-ala'* (الآلاء) means blessings, the plural of *il'* (إلْيٌ), with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the lam, and *ali'* (ألْيٌ), with a fatha on the hamza, a sukun on the lam, and a ya' at its end. It is also said *alw* (ألْوٌ), with a waw in place of the ya'. It means blessing.

The dual pronoun in ﴿your Lord, you both deny﴾ is an address to two groups of those addressed by the Qur'an. In my view, the preferable reading is that it is addressed to the believers and the disbelievers, into which the category of humankind mentioned in His saying ﴿He created man﴾ (Al-Rahman: 3) is divided. They are the ones addressed in His saying ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ (Al-Rahman: 8), and the verse, and the "creatures" (*al-anam*) previously mentioned are divided into them. That is, God's blessings upon people are not denied by a disbeliever, let alone a believer. Each group is addressed by the question in the sense that suits its condition.

The primary purpose is *ta'ridh* (تعريض, allusion) to and rebuke of the polytheists, for associating others in worship with the Benefactor, who is not the Benefactor, and bearing witness against them to the monotheism of the believers. The word *takdhib* (التكذيب, denial) is used in the sense of repudiation and denial.

It has been said that the dual form follows a pattern in Arabic speech where a single person is addressed in the dual form, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾ (Qaf: 24). Al-Tabari and al-Nasafi mentioned this.

It is also possible that the dual form stands in place of repeating the word to emphasise the meaning, like *labbayka wa sa'dayka* (لبيّكَ وسعديك, "at your service, and again at your service"). The meaning of this is that the address is to one person, who is the human being.

The majority of exegetes said: it is an address to humankind and the jinn. This is far-fetched, because the Qur'an was revealed to address and admonish people, and it did not come to address the jinn. Therefore the Qur'an does not address them directly. What is reported in the Qur'an about a group of jinn being guided by the Qur'an, in Surat al-Ahqaf and in Surat al-Jinn, is understood to mean that God obligated the jinn to follow what becomes clear to them according to their comprehension. God may obligate categories of beings with what only they are fit for, to the exclusion of others, just as He obligated the people of knowledge to reflect on doctrines and to exert independent reasoning (*ijtihad*) in the branches of law, and did not obligate the common people with that. So whatever is mentioned in the Qur'an about the jinn is in the context of relating God's dealings with them, and not for directing the practice of the Sharia.

As for what al-Tirmidhi narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari, that the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to his companions and recited to them Surat al-Rahman while they were silent. He said to them: "I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they were better in their response than you. Every time I came to His saying ﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾, they said: 'None of Your blessings, our Lord, do we deny, and to You belongs all praise.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: this is a *gharib* (غريب, rare) hadith. Its chain includes Zuhayr ibn Muhammad, whom al-Bukhari and Ahmad ibn Hanbal declared weak.

Even if this hadith is sound, it is not an explanation of the dual pronoun, because the jinn heard it after its revelation, so it does not entail that they are the ones addressed by it. They were only following those whom God addressed. It has been said that the address is to males and females, but this is far-fetched.

The word *takdhib* is used figuratively in the sense of repudiation and denial, to make this repudiation appear abhorrent.

The denial of the blessings (*takdhib al-ala'*) is a *kinaya* (كناية, metonymy) for associating others with God in divinity. The meaning is: "Then by which of God's blessings upon you will you deny that it is a blessing upon you, so that you associate others with Him in it? Indeed, you deny all His blessings, since you worship other than Him continually."

This is a transition to reflection on God's creation of man and His creation of the jinn.

The discussion of the predicate's placement is similar to the discussion of His saying ﴿The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Rahman: 2].

By "man" (al-insan) is meant Adam, who is the origin of the species. His saying "from clay (salsal)" has a parallel that was discussed in Surat al-Hijr.

Salsal is dry clay.

Fakhkhar is clay that has been fired by fire, and is called pottery (khazaf). The apparent sense of the exegetes' statements is that His saying "like pottery" is an attribute of "salsal." Al-Kawashi explicitly stated this in Talkhis al-Tabsira, and they did not give attention to the benefit of this description. What appears to me is that "like pottery" should be a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "man," meaning: He created him from dry clay, so man became like pottery in a particular form and hardness.

The meaning that it is dry clay resembling the dryness of fired clay is that the one compared is not the same as the one compared to. He expressed it with "black mud shaped (hama' masnun)," "sticky clay (tin lazib)," and "dust (turab)."

Al-jann is the jinn, and by it is meant Iblis and the devils who descended from him. God has related his saying: ﴿You created me from fire, and You created him from clay﴾ [al-A'raf: 12].

Al-marij is that which is mixed. It is an active participle used in the sense of a passive participle, like "dafiq" and "'ishatun radiyah." That is, He created the jinn from a mixture of fire, meaning mixed with other elements, except that fire predominates in it, just as dust predominated in the constitution of man, along with what he has of the element of fire, which is the innate heat (al-hararah al-ghariziyyah).

The intended subject here is the creation of man, as indicated by the closing phrase ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 13]. It was paired with the creation of the jinn only to show the perfection of the blessing in the creation of man from a soft material, receptive to refinement and perfection, and to show the gentleness that comes from him toward the creatures that are with him on the face of the earth.

It is also a reminder and an admonition through one of the manifestations of God's power and wisdom in the creation of the human species and the jinn kind.

It also contains an allusion to what preceded in the Qur'an revealed before this surah concerning the preference of man over the jinn, when God commanded the jinn to prostrate to man, and what that implies of the abundance of human benefits over the benefits of the jinn, and of his qualification to populate the world because he was created from its clay, since excellence results from a combination of attributes, not from single particularities.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

This is a rebuke for failing to acknowledge the blessings of God Most High. It is phrased in the same way as its counterpart that preceded it, so that the rebuke takes the form of speech like its predecessor. This kind of repetition in the style of rebuke, and similar, is when the expression is like the preceding speech; so it is more fitting to call this iteration (ta'dad) rather than repetition (takrir), since it is not repetition merely for emphasis. The fa' in His words ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 18] here is a consequence of His words ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17], because His lordship necessitates acknowledging Him for the blessing of creation and provision. From the similarity of the repeated sentences there also results the benefit of emphasis and confirmation; so the repetition has two purposes, as we mentioned earlier in the discussion of the beginning of the surah.

The benefit of the repetition is to reinforce the affirmation of the blessings God Most High has bestowed upon the addressees, and to allude to rebuking them for associating with God idols that possess no blessing for anyone, all of which are proofs of the unique divinity (tafarrud al-ilahiyya). It is related from Ibn Qutaybah that God enumerated in this surah blessings, and mentioned His creation of His favours, then followed every attribute He described and every blessing He set down with this phrase, and made it a separator between every two blessings, in order to alert them to the blessings and make them acknowledge them. End of quotation. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: repetition is a driving away of heedlessness and a confirmation of the proof.

Al-Sharif al-Murtada said in his Majalis and Amali, called al-Durar wa al-Ghurar: This is abundant in the speech and poetry of the Arabs. Muhalhil ibn Rabi'ah said, lamenting his brother Kulayb:

"Is it not an injustice of Kulayb that, when he drove the orphan away from the slaughtered camel..."

He mentioned the first half-line eight times at the beginnings of consecutive verses. And al-Harith ibn 'Abbad said:

"Bring the tethering-post of the ostrich closer to me, / the war of Wa'il has given birth, so draw near to the ropes"

Then he repeated his saying, "Bring the tethering-post of the ostrich closer to me," in many verses of the qasida.

The same applies to the counterparts of His words ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ mentioned here, up to what is at the end of the surah.

Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests.

This is a fresh (ibtida'i) resumptive sentence (isti'naf), which explains the phrase "The sun and the moon [move] by calculation" (Ar-Rahman: 5). The phrase "and Lord of the two wests" is conjoined (ʿataf) for the reason I mentioned just above, namely observing the pairing (muzawaja).

The subject (musnad ilayhi) is elided in the manner that al-Sakkaki (al-Sakkakī) termed following the established usage that omits it, or omits its counterparts, and this has been discussed more than once before.

Al-mashriq (the east) is the direction from which the sun rises, and al-maghrib (the west) is the direction in which it sets. The dual forms "two easts" and "two wests" are used because the sun rises in winter and spring from one point on the horizon, and in summer and autumn from another point, and because of the difference between the time of long days and the time of short days. Likewise, its setting: between these two easts and two wests, its rising and setting shift through closely adjacent degrees. Accordingly, it may be considered, and it is said: "the easts" and "the wests," as in His Exalted saying: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests, indeed We are able﴾ (Al-Ma'arij: 40), in Surat al-Ma'arij.

As for one who claims that the dual form "two easts" is used to account for the east of the sun and the moon, and likewise the dual "two wests," he has not delved into a great meaning.

According to what the majority of scholars (al-jumhur) explained "the two easts" and "the two wests" as the eastern and western points of the sun, then by "the two easts" is meant the eastern half of the earth, and by "the two wests" the western half of it.

The lordship (rububiyya) of God Most High over the two easts and the two wests is in the sense of creation and disposal (al-takharruf).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verse 19–20:

﴿He released the two seas, meeting each other﴾ ﴿between them is a barrier which they do not transgress﴾.

Another statement about the All-Merciful, whose purpose is to draw attention to the creation of seas and rivers, which is a wondrous creation that points to the greatness of Allah's power, knowledge and wisdom.

The reason for mentioning it after what precedes it is that, when He mentioned that He, glory be to Him, is the Lord of the two easts and the Lord of the two wests, and the seas and rivers are in the regions of the earth, it was appropriate to move on to taking heed of His creating them both and to the favour of what He deposited in them of benefits for people.

Al-maraj (مَرَج) has many meanings, and the first of them in this discourse is release, from the saying "maraja al-dabbah" (he let the animal loose), when he released it to graze in the maraj, which is the wide land with pasture that has no owner, i.e., leaving it to go wherever it wishes.

The meaning is: He released the two seas, not restraining their water from flowing by any barrier. This is a preparation for His saying after ﴿they meet﴾: ﴿between them is a barrier which they do not transgress﴾.

What is intended is that He created them and released them, for He released them only after creating them.

Yaltaqiyan (يَلْتَقِيانِ): they join, such that one of them pours into the other.

Al-bahr (البَحْر): the water that covers a great part of the earth, and it is applied to both salt and sweet water.

What is meant by the dual is the two kinds of sea, namely the salt sea and the sweet sea, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink, and this one is salty, bitter﴾ [Fatir: 12]. The definiteness is definiteness of the generic known (ta'rif al-'ahd al-jinsi).

So what is intended is what the Arabs know of these two kinds, namely the river Euphrates and the Persian Sea, which is today called the Persian Gulf. Their meeting is the pouring of the water of the Euphrates into the Persian Gulf at the shore of Basra, and the lands on the Arab shore of the Persian Gulf are known among the Arabs as the lands of Bahrain for this reason.

What is meant by the barrier between them is the separating partition between the sweet and salt waters, such that neither of the two seas changes the taste of the other by its proximity. This is due to the properties in each of the waters which prevent the other from mixing with it. This is among the matters of specific gravity. The mention of the barrier is an eloquent simile: i.e., between them is something like a barrier, and this is the meaning of ﴿they do not transgress﴾, i.e., neither of them transgresses upon the other, meaning that one does not overpower the other and spoil its taste. The word "baghy" (transgression), whose true meaning is aggression and oppression, is borrowed for this overpowering.

It is also possible that the dual is the dual of two specific salt seas, and the definiteness is then the definiteness of the present known (ta'rif al-'ahd al-huduri). So what is meant is two seas known to the Arabs. The most apparent view is that what is meant is the Red Sea, on whose shores lie the coasts of Tihamah, such as Jeddah and Yanbu' al-Nakhl, and the Sea of Oman, which is the Arabian Sea, on whose shores lie Hadramawt and Aden of the lands of Yemen. Al-barzakh (البَرْزَخ): the separating barrier, and the barrier between these two seas is the strait of Bab al-Mandab, where the port of Aden and the port of Zeila are located.

Since the creation of the two seas contains great blessings for people, some of them known to all of them, for they travel upon them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you see the ships ploughing through it﴾ [al-Nahl: 14], and He said: ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea﴾ [Yunus: 22], and the extraction of their fish and purification with their water. Some of them are known to the scholars, namely the effect of the salts of the sea on purifying the air of the earth, drawing down rain, and attracting the bodies that fall from the shooting stars, and other than that.

The clause "yaltaqiyan" and the clause "between them is a barrier" are two circumstantial clauses (hal) referring to the two seas.

The clause "la yabghiyan" (they do not transgress) explains the clause "between them is a barrier."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verse 24:

﴿And His are the ships, raised high upon the sea like landmarks.﴾

The sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence ﴿From them come forth the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], because this belongs to the conditions of the two seas. The repetition of the word "the sea" has dispensed with a pronoun referring to "the two seas" that would link the circumstantial clause to its subject.

The lam here indicates ownership (al-milk), and it is the ownership of subjugating the sailing upon them. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And among His signs are the ships running upon the sea like landmarks﴾ [al-Shura: 32], and ﴿If He wills, He stills the winds, so they become motionless upon its surface. Indeed in that are signs for everyone patient and grateful﴾ [al-Shura: 33], or ﴿He wrecks them because of what they have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 34]. The meaning is that the ships on the sea are under His disposal, exalted is He. He says: ﴿And the ship runs upon the sea by His command﴾ [al-Hajj: 65].

The information that the ships belong to Him serves as an alert that the creation of the sea for ships does not take them out of the ownership of Allah.

The word "al-jawari" (the running ones) is an adjective of a deleted noun indicated by its complement, which is His saying: "upon the sea." The estimate is: "the ships, the running ones," since nothing runs upon the sea except ships.

In the Imam Mushaf, al-jawari is written with a ra at its end without a ya. Its analogical spelling would be with a ya at its end, but it was written without a ya, taking into account the state of its pronunciation in continuous recitation (wasl), since the reader does not pause on it. For this reason all ten readers recite it without a ya in both continuous recitation and pause, because pausing on it is rare in the recitation of the two readers.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read al-munshaʾat with a fatha on the shin, so it is a passive participle (ism maf'ul), meaning when it is brought into existence and made, i.e., those which people have produced through inspiration from Allah. Thus two favors arise from the speech: the favor of subjugating the ships to sail upon the sea, and the favor of inspiring people to produce them.

Hamza and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read it with a kasra on the shin, so it is an active participle (ism fa'il).

It is permissible that al-munshaʾat be derived from "ansa'a al-sayr" (he made the travel), when he hastened, i.e., those by which people travel swiftly. Mujahid said: "al-munshaʾat are those whose sails have been raised." The verse admits both meanings according to the two readings, by using the derivation in both senses of the source word, and in this there is a reminder of the favor of Allah's inspiring people to invent the sail to speed the sailing of ships, and it is among what was invented after the building of Noah's ark.

The ships are described as being "like landmarks," i.e., mountains, a description which conveys the magnification of their status in their construction, which requires the wondrousness of the inspiration of human minds to build them, and which requires the greatness of the favor in them, because ships are better able to carry large numbers of people and goods.

The sentence is an independent, initiatory resumption (istinaf ibtida'i).

The intended meaning of (man ʿalayhā) is people, since they are the ones addressed by these lessons; for this reason (man), the relative pronoun specific to rational beings, was used.

The meaning is: the destiny of all who are upon the earth is perishing, and this reminder of death and what follows it of recompense.

And (Wajh Rabbika): His essence. The mention of "face" here is in accordance with the usage of Arabic speech. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "The face is used to express the whole and the essence." End of quote.

The word "face" has been attributed to His Exalted Name in various meanings, of which is what is here, and of which is His saying ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115], and His saying ﴿We feed you only for the sake of Allah's Face﴾ [al-Insan: 9].

The listeners know that it is impossible for Allah the Exalted to have a face in the literal sense, which is the part located in the head.

The scholars of creed have agreed to call such things "ambiguous" (mutashabih). The early generation (al-salaf) used to refrain from speculation about this, while holding certainty in the impossibility of the apparent meaning for Allah the Exalted. Then the scholars of the Successors and those after them undertook interpretation gradually, until the manner of interpretation became clear by proceeding according to the rules of the science of ma'ani (semantics of eloquence), so the obscurity dissipated, the harshness was removed, and both groups were among the best of the upright (hanifs).

The pronoun of address in His saying "(Wajhu Rabbika)" is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and in it is exaltation of the rank of the Prophet ﷺ, as has been mentioned more than once.

The intention is that it be conveyed to those to whom the Qur'an is recited, so that they may be reminded and take heed. It is also permissible that it be an address to an unspecified addressee, so as to include every person addressed.

Since the face here means the essence, it is described as ﴿Possessor of Majesty﴾, meaning greatness, ﴿and Honor﴾, meaning the Bestower of blessings upon His servants. Otherwise, the literal face is not attributed to honor in the usage of the language; rather, it is the hand that is attributed to honor. That is, He does not deprive His servants of His majesty and His generosity.

Within "Majesty" is included every attribute that returns to His transcendence above deficiency, and within "Honor" is included every attribute of perfection that pertains to existence and attributes of beauty such as benevolence.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verse 29:**

﴿Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Him.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement and is not grammatically linked to what precedes it). The meaning is that generations of people pass away and other generations remain, and everything that remains needs the means of its continuance and the soundness of its conditions. Thus they are in need of the One who does not perish, and He has no need of them. When the report reached the point of people's need of Him, exalted is He, it was followed by the statement that need is general, encompassing the people of the earth and the people of the heavens. All of them ask Him. The asking of the people of the heavens, who are the angels, consists in their glorifying their Lord with His praise, seeking forgiveness for those on the earth, and asking for the pleasure of God, exalted is He. The asking of those on the earth, who are human beings, consists in their asking Him for the blessings of life, for deliverance in the Hereafter, and for the raising of ranks in the Hereafter. The object of *yas'aluhu* has been omitted to convey generality, meaning they ask Him for their needs and their concerns from sunrise until sunset.

* * *

﴿Every day He is in a matter.﴾

It is permissible for this sentence to be a *hal* (circumstantial clause, a clause describing the state of the subject or object at the time of the action) from the pronoun of object in *yas'aluhu*, or a *tadhyil* (a concluding sentence that adds a general truth after a statement) to the sentence ﴿Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾. That is, every day He is in a matter among the matters, [Page 255] for the askers and for others. He, exalted is He, carries out various affairs concerning the states of existing things, continuously. The phrase "every day" (*kull yawm*) is a adverbial of time (*zarf*) connected to the stative verb (*istiqrar*) in His saying ﴿He is in a matter﴾. It has been placed before the item to which it is related, for the sake of emphasis, to convey the recurrence and continuity of this.

The meaning is: He is in a matter among the matters of those in the heavens and the earth, such as the granting of a request, increase, deprivation, delay in granting a request, and compensation for what is missed through a reward. This is as is reported in the hadiths on supplication, that its answer varies. This was mentioned earlier at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Your Lord has said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60].

The meaning of *fi* (in) according to this interpretation is to strengthen the affirmation of the matters for God, exalted is He, and these matters are the matters of His governance and the manifestations of His power. As al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Nisaburi said: "Matters He manifests, not matters He initiates."

The word "day" (*yawm*) is used figuratively for time, by the relation of generality (*'alaqat al-iṭlaq*), since the meaning is: every moment of the times, even for an instant. The intended "day" is not the specific period that extends from dawn to sunset.

The application of "day" and similar words to time in general is common in Arabic speech, as when they say: "The age is two days: a day of blessings and a day of misery." 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*And indeed tomorrow and today are pledged, and after tomorrow is that which you do not know.*

He meant future time, present time, and distant future time, for otherwise what difference is there between "tomorrow" and "after tomorrow"?

The word *sha'n* (matter) means a great thing and an important event, among creatures and actions in the heavens and the earth. In a hadith: "He, exalted is He, every day forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises some people and lowers others." He, exalted is He, commands and forbids, gives life and causes death, gives and withholds, and the like. Since in His governance there is every matter, then what is less than a matter is more appropriately included in His governance.

The sense of *zarfiyya* (being a container, in the sense of location) that is used with the particle *fi* is a figurative sense, borrowed to express the intensity of the involvement with and connection to God's governance, like the encompassing of the container around the contained, or like the questions of the creatures who are in the heavens and the earth.

The meaning is: He, exalted is He, every day, His power relates to matters which He brings forth, and His command of creation relates to matters of bringing into existence or annihilation.

Among the finest words on the interpretation of this verse is the saying of al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl when 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir asked him, saying: "This saying of His has become unclear to me, and it is established that the Pen has dried up with what is to exist until the Day of Resurrection." He said: "They are matters He manifests, not matters He initiates." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl gave a concise answer that satisfies the likes of 'Abd Allah ibn Tahir, although the difficulty does not arise, since the verse does not say that the matters contradict what the Pen of Divine Knowledge has inscribed. Moreover, this answer applies only to one of the interpretations of His saying ﴿every day He is in a matter﴾, as you have just learned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verse 31:

﴿Soon We shall attend to you, O you two burdens.﴾

This is a transition (takhallus) from reflecting on the conditions of the present worldly life to reminding of the conditions of the Hereafter and of the recompense therein. It moved to this by way of connection with what preceded, which contained evidences of the vastness of God the Exalted's power, with an implicit allusion that the one who does such things deserves to be singled out for divinity (tawhid bil-ilahiyya) and deserves to be devoted to worship alone. Since those addressed by this were polytheists alongside God in worship, it moved on to threatening them that they and their allies from the jinn, who embellished the worship of idols for them, will be presented for God's judgment concerning them.

Page 257
The particle of future (harf al-tanfis) is used for the general sense of the construction, which is a metonymy for certainty, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿He said: "I shall ask my Lord to forgive you"﴾ [Yusuf: 98] in Surat Yusuf.

Al-faragh (fara') to something means being free of what occupies one from it, and it is a figurative expression for giving attention to a thing. It likens the state of one who is devoted to one action rather than another to the state of a vessel that has been emptied of what is in it so that it may be filled with something else.

This figure is suitable for use in the sense of attending to something, as in the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq to his son 'Abd al-Rahman: "Fraghu ila adyafika" (Attend to your guests), i.e., be free of every preoccupation so that you may occupy yourself with your guests and devote yourself to their hospitality. It is also suitable for use in the sense of a threat, as in the saying of Jarir:

"Now, since I have turned to Numayr, this is the time when I became a punishment for them."

The sense that fits the context of the verse, considering what precedes and what follows, is that it be understood as the turning to the affairs of the two burdens in the Hereafter, because after it comes ﴿The criminals will be recognized by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41], and this is addressed to the disbelievers of both burdens, who are the majority at the time this verse was revealed.

Al-thaqalan: the dual of thaqal, and this dual noun is a singular noun for the totality of mankind and jinn.

I reckon that the thaqal is the human being, because he is carried upon the earth, so he is like a burden upon a beast; and that the application of this dual to mankind and jinn is by way of predominance (taghlib). Other explanations have been given, but they are not acceptable to one who reflects. This word in this meaning has been counted among those used only in the dual form, so the term thaqal is not applied to the human species alone; hence it is a dual in form but singular in application. I think this word was not applied to the totality of both species before the Qur'an, so it became one of the proper names of genera by dominance, and then the people of Islam used it. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"Mayya is the most beautiful of the two burdens in face and in neck, and the most beautiful of them in nape."

He intended "wa-ahsanu al-thaqalayn" and made the pronoun referring to it singular. He erred in using it, since the jinn have no connection to any part of his purpose.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sanafrughu" with the letter ya' (yafrughu... ) open, meaning the pronoun refers to God the Exalted, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). The majority read it with nun.

Page 258
The word "ayyuha" is written in the Mushaf with a ha' that has no alif after it; this is an orthographic convention that takes into account the pronunciation of the word in connected speech (wasl), since one does not stop on such a form. The majority read it with a fatha on the ha' without an alif in both connected and pause states. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with an alif after the ha' in pause. Ibn 'Amir read the ha' with a damma, following the damma of the ya' before it, and this is an instance of assimilation of vowels (ittiba').

The repetition of this phrase in its sister passages. It is not addressed to both jinn and humankind (al-thaqalan), nor is it a concluding refrain (tadhyil) for the sentence before it, since the sentence before it does not mention any blessing upon the two groups; rather, that sentence is a warning (tahdid) to them both.

This is the object of an omitted verb of speech, which the context before and after indicates, and it is not an address to humans and jinn in this worldly life. The implied sense is: "So We will say to you, as in His saying, ﴿And on the day He gathers them all, [He will say], 'O assembly of jinn, you have taken much from mankind'﴾ [al-An'am: 128], etc.," meaning: "O assembly of jinn, you have taken much from mankind." This was discussed earlier in Surat al-An'am.

Al-Ma'shar (the assembly) is a noun for a large group that is counted in tens, not individually.

This is a proclamation to them that they are in the grip of God, the Exalted, and find no escape from it. It is also a warning to the misguided and the misleaders, among the jinn and mankind, of the evil recompense awaiting them. Such a phrase is not addressed to a mixed group unless the intended target is the guilty among them. Therefore His saying ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind﴾ is general in wording but particular in meaning, as indicated by His following words ﴿There will be sent against you both a flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 35], etc.

Al-Nufudh and al-Nafadh (penetrating, passing through) mean that something passes through another thing and exits from it. The conditional clause is used to express incapacity, and likewise the command that is the answer to this condition, in His saying ﴿then pass through﴾, meaning: "while you are unable to flee."

Page 259

The meaning is: "If you are able to slip out of this position, then slip out." This implies an allusive warning of the punishment that will appear in that position for the people of misguidance.

Al-aqtar (the regions) is the plural of qutr, with a dammah on the qaf and a sukun on the ta', meaning the wide side of a broad place. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿and if it had been entered upon them from its regions﴾ [al-Ahzab: 14], in Surat al-Ahzab.

He mentions the heavens and the earth to establish that all directions surround them, as confirmation of the incapacity: "Here are the heavens and the earth before you. If you are able, then exit from one direction of them to flee from this position of yours, since multiplicity of places makes escape from one of their directions easier."

The earth mentioned here may be either the earth known in this world, at the time of resurrection, or the earth of the gathering, which the Qur'an called al-Sahirah in Surat al-Nazi'at. He, the Exalted, said ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth, and the heavens [as well]﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]. Or it may be that this runs in the manner of a proverb used for emphasis on the encompassing of all directions, like the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: "What earth would carry me, and what sky would shade me?"

These meanings do not contradict one another, and they are among the aspects of the Qur'an's inimitability.

The clause ﴿you will not pass through except by authority﴾ explains the incapacity expressed in the clause before it. Authority (sultan) means power, meaning: "You will not pass out of this predicament except by a great power that exceeds the power of God, who gathered you to this position. And from where would you have such strength?"

This follows the pattern of His saying ﴿The devils did not bring it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 210], ﴿and it is not fitting for them, nor are they able [to do so]﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 211], meaning: they did not ascend to the heaven so as to bring it down.

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) following the phrase ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through﴾ [al-Rahman: 33] and so on, because that hint of threat stirs in their souls a question about what lies beyond it.

The pronoun in ﴿عَلَيْكُما﴾ ("against you both") refers to the jinn and humankind. It is general in form but is intended in a specific sense, by the indication (qarina) of His words that follow: ﴿But for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46] and the verses after it. This is an explicit statement that they will be punished, after an allusion to that had been made by His words ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through﴾ [al-Rahman: 33].

The meaning of ﴿يُرْسَلُ عَلَيْكُما﴾ ("will be sent against you both") is that this will confront them before they enter Hell, i.e., you will be pelted with a flame of fire as a hastening of the evil. The present tense (al-mudari') indicates the present: "and a flame of fire is being sent against you both now."

Shuwaz (شُواظ), with the shin vowelled either with a damma or a kasra, is a flame that is not mixed with smoke, because its burning has become complete, and that is more intensely scorching. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a damma on the shin. Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra.

Nuhas (نُحاس) is applied to smoke that has no flame with it. Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr interpreted it this way, and al-Khalil followed them.

The meaning on this reading is that the smoke, by which they are not harmed and do not suffocate because of the intensity of the flame of the shuwaz, is added to that shuwaz as a separate thing, so they escape neither of the two.

Nuhas is also applied to ṣufr (صُفْر), which is brass (qitr). Mujahid and Qatada interpreted it this way, and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning then is that molten brass is poured over them.

The majority read ﴿وَنُحاسٌ﴾ with a raised vowel (al-raf'), in coordination (ʿatf) with ﴿شُواظٌ﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Rawh from Ya'qub read it in the genitive (majrur), in coordination with ﴿نارٍ﴾. In that case the shuwaz is also from it: that is, a flame of fire from a fire, and a flame of molten brass. This is a fire that breaks the customary order, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿Its fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24].

The meaning of ﴿فَلا تَنْتَصِرانِ﴾ ("and you will have no defender") is: you will find no escape from that, and you will find no helper.

The word "helper" (al-nasir) here is meant in both its literal and figurative senses, i.e., you will find no one who repels that from you, and no refuge by which you may protect yourselves.

It is a repetition (takrir), like what was said about the one that occurred shortly before it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verses 37–40:

﴿And when the sky splits open and becomes red like a rose, like oil dregs.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿On that day, neither man nor jinn will be asked about his sin.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') following on from a previously mentioned report, namely the general statement in His words ﴿We will soon attend to you, O two burdens﴾ [al-Rahman: 31] and so on to the end. It is a detailed explanation of that generality (ijmal), by specifying its time, some of the terrors that will befall the criminals in it, and the good tidings of the bliss and joy that the God-fearing will be given.

His words ﴿and it became a rose﴾ are an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), meaning: it became like a rose.

The rose (wardah) is a single flower of the roses (ward), a red blossom of a thin shrub with thorny branches that appears in the spring and is well known. As for the point of resemblance, it has been said that it is the intensity of redness: the colour of the sky, which is known to be blue, turns to white, and so its colour becomes red. God says ﴿On the day the earth will be changed into other than the earth, and the heavens too﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]. It is also possible in my view that the point of resemblance is the abundance of cracks, like the petals of a rose.

Al-dihan, with a kasra on the dal, is the sediment of oil (durdi al-zayt). This is a second simile for the sky, in respect of its undulating and turbulent motion.

The clause ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the conditional clause (shart) and the response clause (jawab). It was cited in Mughni al-Labib (Mughni al-Labib, by Ibn Hisham) as an example of an insertion between the condition and its response, and he identified it as a parenthetical insertion and not a circumstantial clause (hal). This clause is a parenthetical insertion of repetition, for affirmation and rebuke, as is clear. The splitting of the sky is among the circumstances of the Gathering, meaning: when the Resurrection occurs and the sky splits open, as He says ﴿Then on that day the Inevitable will occur﴾ [al-Haqqah: 15] ﴿and the sky will split open﴾ [al-Haqqah: 16], and His words ﴿On that day you will be presented, and none of your secrets will be hidden﴾ [al-Haqqah: 18]. This is the splitting mentioned in His words ﴿On the day the sky will split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25] ﴿Sovereignty on that day belongs truly to the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 26] in surah al-Furqan.

The meaning of ﴿will not be asked about his sin﴾ is the negation of the kind of questioning in which the questioner intends to learn whether the uncertain matter has occurred. This is like His words ﴿and the guilty will not be asked about their sins﴾ [al-Qasas: 78].

It is not the questioning in His words ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92] ﴿about what they used to do﴾ [al-Hijr: 93], and His words ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]. That is for affirmation and rebuke. The Day of Resurrection has a long span of time, so there are stations in which the people of sins will not be asked about their sins, and there are stations in which they will be questioned with questioning for affirmation and rebuke.

The clause ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ is a repetition for affirmation and rebuke.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verses 43–44:

﴿This is Hell, which the criminals used to deny.﴾ ﴿They will go around between it and scalding, boiling water.﴾

This is what will be said on the Day of Resurrection before the assembled multitude.

Describing Hell as ﴿which the criminals used to deny﴾ is a way of making the criminals look foolish and exposing them. The clause "yatufuna" (they go around) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to "al-mujrimun" (the criminals), meaning that the foolishness of their denial of Hell has become clearly evident, through its becoming visible to people and through their moving back and forth within it, just as they moved back and forth in denying it when they were warned of it in the worldly life.

Al-tawaf (circumambulation/going around) is repeated walking and frequent movement around something. One says "taafa bihi" and "taafa 'alayhi." From it comes the tawaf around the Ka'bah and the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿There is no sin upon him for going around between them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], and this was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-hamim (scalding water) is water that has been heated to an intense degree of heat.

This is like His saying: ﴿And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

"An" (ANin) is an active participle from "anā," meaning that its heat has become intense.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

Its position in the repetition is like the position of the one before it.

[Page 265]

This is a transition from describing the requital of the criminals to the reward of the God-fearing. The sentence is coordinated (*'atf*) with the sentence ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41] and what follows it, and this is the more evident reading, because His saying at its end, ﴿They will go around between it and scalding hot water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44], conveys that they are within it.

The *lam* in *liman* ("for whoever") is the *lam* of ownership (*lam al-milk*), meaning: whoever fears his Lord is given and made the owner of two gardens. There is no doubt that *man* ("whoever") *khafa maqama rabbihi* refers to the category of those who fear, not to a specific fearer. It is therefore one of the forms of substitutive generality (*al-'umum al-badali*), like your saying: "For the one who fears is the standing of his Lord." On this basis, the question arises regarding the interpretation of the dual *jannatan* ("two gardens"). It is possible that what is meant is two kinds of gardens.

The gardens have been mentioned in the Qur'an in the plural form on more than one occasion, and after this will come His saying ﴿And besides them are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 62], so what is meant is two kinds of gardens.

It is also possible that the dual is used figuratively (*kinaya*, metonymy) to denote multiplicity. This usage exists in eloquent speech and in the Qur'an. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then return your gaze twice; your gaze will return to you humbled and weary﴾ [al-Mulk: 4].

From this usage is their saying: *labbayka* and *sa'dayka* and *dawalayka* ("at your service, again and again"), like the verse of al-Qawwal al-Ta'i from the *Hamasa* poetry:

*So say to this man, who has come running: "Come! For the sharp swords are the obligations."*

That is, "So say: O people." This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿We will punish them twice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 101] in Surah al-Tawbah. The choice of the dual form here is for the sake of observing the *fawasil* (verse-endings, the rhyme-pattern, singular *fasila*) both before and after it, since the rhyme-patterns of the surah are built upon it, and the rhyme-pattern is evident. This is also the view inclined to by al-Farra's statement. On this basis, all that is expressed in the dual form concerning the two gardens is meant in the plural sense.

It has also been said: what is meant is two gardens for each God-fearing person, encircling his palace within Paradise, as God, exalted is He, said in describing the worldly gardens: ﴿We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines﴾ [al-Kahf: 32], and the verse, and He said: ﴿There was for Sheba in their dwelling a sign: two gardens, on the right and on the left﴾ [Saba': 15]. So they are two gardens with respect to the right and left sides of the palace, and the palace separates them.

As for *al-maqam* ("the standing/station"): its original meaning is the place of standing, and it is a *mimi* verbal noun (a noun beginning with *mim*) from standing. On both understandings it is used metaphorically for a state or condition, as when you say to someone whose protection you seek: "This is the station of one who seeks refuge in you."
