Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verse 54:

﴿Reclining on couches lined with brocade, and the fruit of the two gardens will be within reach.﴾

It is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to ﴿for those who fear the standing before their Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]. The circumstantial element is put in the plural form to account for the referent's meaning and the capacity of its wording to denote both the singular and the plural, not in view of the fact that its relative clause is in the singular form, since that would be a consideration of the word "man" (مَن) being singular in form.

The meaning is: they are given the gardens, they settle in them, and they recline upon couches.

Al-ittika' (reclining) is an ifti'al form derived from al-wak' (with a hamzated final radical), which means reliance. Thus al-ittika' became a term for the seated person's leaning of his elbow and side upon the ground, a posture between lying on one's side and sitting. This has been discussed in His words ﴿and she prepared for them a reclining couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31] in Surah Yusuf, and also previously in Surah al-Saffat.

Furush (couches) is the plural of firash, like kitab and kutub. The original sense of firash is that which is spread out (yufrash), i.e., laid down upon the ground for sleeping and reclining.

Then the term firash was applied to a raised bed set on legs, because what is normally spread on the ground is placed upon it, a naming by the name of what is contained in it. For this reason its mention occurs in Surah al-Waqi'ah in His words ﴿on beds woven with gold and silver﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15], ﴿reclining upon them, facing one another﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 16], and in Surah al-Saffat ﴿on couches facing one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 44].

What is referred to in these verses is one and the same, which indicates that the intended meaning of "furush" in this verse is the beds upon which the couches are placed.

Al-ittika' is the sitting posture of the pampered, served people, because it is a posture of ease and of not needing to rise for taking food and the like. It was discussed in Surah al-Kahf.

Al-bata'in (linings) is the plural of bitanah, with a kasra on the ba', derived from al-batn (the belly), the opposite of al-zahr (the back) of anything. Here it is used metaphorically for the lower part. The lower side is called batn, and the upper side is called zahr. One says: "I lined my garment with another" (batanat thawbi bi-akhar) when one places another garment beneath one's garment. So the lining (bitanah) of a garment is its inner part and what does not show of it. The opposite of bitanah is ziharah with a kasra on the zay. Among their expressions is: "The back and belly of his affair spread me out (afrashani zahr amrihi wa batnuhu)," meaning its openness and its secret. The openness was likened to the top of a couch and the secret to its underside, these being the zihara and the bitana. For this reason the metaphor of the verb afrashani was followed by this comparison. So bitanah is the cloth placed on the couch, and zihārah is the cloth placed over the bitanah so that it is visible to one who sees the inside of the house; thus zihārah is better than bitanah in a single couch.

The Arabs used to make the couch a hashiyah, that is, something stuffed with wool, cotton or palm fibre so that it would be softer for the side. 'Antarah said, describing 'Abla's luxury:

She spends the evening and the morning upon the back of a hashiyah, while I spend the night upon the back of a bay, bridled steed.

When they place a cloth over the hashiyah or sew it with a cloth, that is the bitanah; and when they cover that with a cloth finer than it, that is the zihārah.

The meaning here is that the linings of the couches of Paradise are of brocade, so do not ask about their outer surfaces, for they are finer than that. No garment among the garments known to people in this world is more precious than the brocade of the linings. Mentioning the linings specifically is a metaphor (kinayah) for the preciousness of the description of the outer surfaces of the couches.

Al-istabraq: a fine, high-grade kind of thick dibaj. Dibaj: a thick woven fabric of silk, and istabraq is woven with threads of gold. Al-Fakhr said: it is arabicized from the Persian word (stabark), with a kaf at its end as a diminutive marker, (stabaz), meaning thick, and it was discussed in Surah al-Kahf. They changed the kaf into a qaf out of fear of confusing it with the kaf of address. What is in al-Qamus is: al-istabraq: thick dibaj, arabicized from istarwah. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verse 60:

[p. 271]

﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ This is a concluding summary (tadhyil) of the sentences that begin with His words ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46], meaning: because they did good, their Lord rewarded them with good.

The first "good" (ihsan) is the good deed (al-fi'l al-hasan), and the second "good" (ihsan) is the bestowing of what is good, which is benefit (al-khayr). The first derives from the expression "they did well in such-and-such" (ahsanu fi kadha), and the second from the expression "he did good to so-and-so" (ahsana ila fulan).

The interrogative is used here in the sense of negation, and for this reason it is followed by the exception (istithna'), which conveys the restriction (hasr) of the recompense for good to being good. This restriction is an informing that it is the true reward and the requirement of wisdom (hikmah) and justice ('adl). Otherwise, that may fail to occur among the wrongdoers. God the Exalted says: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny [it]﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82], and He says: ﴿But when He gave them a righteous [child], they attributed to Him partners in what He had given them﴾ [al-A'raf: 190].

It is understood from this that the recompense for evil is evil. God the Exalted says: ﴿A recompense in accordance [with their deeds]﴾ [al-Naba': 26].

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr) on Surah 55, verses 62–69:

﴿And besides these two there are two gardens.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿Dark green.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿In them are two fountains gushing forth.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ ﴿In them is fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates.﴾ ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

This is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with His saying "two gardens," meaning: besides those two gardens there are two gardens, for those who fear the standing before their Lord.

The phrase "besides these two" (*min dūnihimā*) may be understood with *dūn* meaning *ghayr* (other than), so that: for those who fear the standing before their Lord there are two gardens, and two other gardens besides them, as in His saying, ﴿For those who do good is the best reward, and more﴾ [Yūnus: 26]. What is in these two gardens is described with a description close to that of the first two, a description in which the method of *iṭnāb* (elaboration and expansion) is also followed, to show their beauty, as an encouragement to strive to attain them through the fear of God, the Exalted. This is what necessitates the repetition of some attributes, or something close to repetition through synonyms.

It may also be that there are, for every one of the four gardens, *ḥūr* (dark-eyed companions) who are "restrained" (*maqṣūrāt*), not moving out of their mansions.

It is also permissible that *dūn* means "less" (*aqall*), i.e. lower in rank: for those who fear the standing before their Lord there are two gardens less than the first two. This implies that these two gardens are for another group of those who feared the standing before their Lord, who are lower than the first in the degree of fear of God, the Exalted.

Perhaps these two gardens belong to the People of the Right (*aṣḥāb al-yamīn*), mentioned in Surah al-Wāqiʿa, and the two gardens mentioned before them in His saying "two gardens … possessing branches" through to the end of the description belong to the Foremost (*al-sābiqūn*), mentioned in Surah al-Wāqiʿa in His saying, ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 10], and the verses that follow.

*Mudhāmmatān* is a descriptive adjective derived from *al-duhma* (with a *ḍamma* on the *dāl*), which is the colour of blackness. He described the two gardens with blackness as an exaggeration of the intensity of the greenness of their trees, to the point that, owing to the close interlacing of their trees and the strength of their greenness, they appear like the two blacks, because when a tree is lush its leaves' greenness intensifies until it approaches black. Abū Tammām took up this meaning and built upon it, saying:

O my two companions, scrutinise your gaze, you will see how the faces of the earth are shaped.

You will see a sunny day that resembles the blossoms of the hills, so that it is as if it were moonlit.

And ﴿*naḍḍākhatān*﴾ means "two gushing forth with water." *Al-naḍḥ* with a *khāʾ* at its end is stronger than *al-naḍḥ* with an unpointed *ḥāʾ*, which is sprinkling.

Here the two fountains (*al-ʿaynān*) are described with other than the attributes used for the two fountains in the two gardens mentioned earlier. It has also been said that the two descriptions are the same, and in that case the difference between the two categories in descriptions is a matter of *tafannun* (variety of expression).

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾

This is a repetition at the end of the descriptions, for the sake of further affirmation and rebuke.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 55, verse 76:

﴿Reclining on green cushions and beautiful Abqari carpets.﴾

(Muttaki'in): a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]. It is repeated without a conjunction because it occurs in a context of enumerating blessings, and that context calls for repetition as a fresh resumption (isti'naf).

Al-Raf-raf: a kind of spread, and it is a collective noun (ism jam') whose singular is raf-rafah, meaning that which is spread over a bed for one to sleep upon. These are woven in the likeness of gardens, and green predominates in them. For this reason Dhu al-Rummah likened gardens to the Abqari spreads in his saying:

Page 275

﴿Until it is as if the gardens of the sandy plain have been clothed by it with the embroidery of Abqar, a covering and a spreading.﴾

So describing them in the verse as (khudr), green, is a descriptive epithet (wasf kashif) that evokes the green color, because it delights the beholder.

Green garments were rare, and they were the clothing of kings and nobles. Al-Nabighah said:

﴿They guard bodies whose delight is ancient, with sleeves of pure cloth and green shoulders.﴾

Garments were dyed with fast colors that washing would not remove, but these were rare because fast dyes were few, and they hardly went beyond green and red; the purple (al-urjuwani) is also called among them.

As for the commonly used dyes of garments among the Arabs, these were what was dyed with wars (a plant dye) and saffron, which yields yellow. Apart from that, the color of the cloth was the color of the material it was woven from: white or black sheep's wool, or camel's hair, or white linen, or black goat's hair.

(﴿Hisan﴾ [al-Rahman: 70]): the plural of hasna', and it is an adjective of raf-raf, since the latter is a collective noun.

(﴿Abqari﴾): a description of what is outstanding in its category and rare in existence. It is a relative adjective (nisbah) to Abqar, pronounced with a fatha, then sukun, then fatha, the name of the land of the jinn in the belief of the Arabs. They attributed to it everything that exceeded the usual in perfection and beauty, until it seemed as if it were not among the known kinds on the earth of mankind. Zuhayr said:

﴿With horses upon which is a jinn-like Abqari quality, deserving someday to attain and to rise above.﴾

This usage spread, so al-Abqari became a description of the outstanding in its category, as the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the vision he related of the well from which he drew water, then Umar took the buckets (i.e., the sins) from him, and they became a great bucket, and I did not see any Abqari drawing its drawing (fari fariyyah) [Bukhari and Muslim]. 

To this al-Ma'arri alluded in his saying:

﴿The masters of eloquence, whenever they saw beauty, counted it among the craft of the jinn.﴾

So the Qur'an struck it as an example of what is familiar to the Arabs in its usage.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you both deny?﴾

This sentence is the last of the repeated refrains, and with it ends the discourse directed toward establishing that God alone bestows blessings and holds sole disposal over affairs.

[Page 277]

﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honor.﴾

This indicates the end of the discourse and serves as a summary of what the surah was built upon: the reminder of God's greatness and His blessings in this world and the Hereafter.

The phrase is an utterance of praise (*thana'*) directed to God, expressed with emphasis through the form *tafa'ala* (*tabaraka*), which, when its verb is not performed by two parties, is intended for intensification (*mubalaghah*).

The meaning is that He is described with perfect blessing. *Barakah* means great good and benefit, and it may also be used to mean elevated rank. This was already discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Furqan.

*Ism* (name) is that which indicates an essence, whether it is a proper name, like the word *Allah*, or a descriptive attribute, like "the Most Beautiful Names" (*al-asma' al-husna*). Thus, whichever of God's names you take, it indicates the essence of God, exalted is He.

He attributed *tabaraka* to *ism*, which is that by which the named is known, rather than saying "Blessed is your Lord," as in His words ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion﴾ [al-Furqan: 1] and His words ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. The intent was to intensify, in the statement, the attribute of blessing through the mode of *kinayah* (metonymy, indirect expression), because it is more eloquent than explicit statement, as is established in the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-ma'ani*). The eloquent have agreed upon this, because if His name is blessed, then His essence is blessed without doubt, since the name indicates the named. This is in the manner of His words ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1], for if glorification is connected to His name, then the connection of glorification to His essence is more fitting. From the same type is His words ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 4], according to the comprehensive interpretation, and the words of 'Antarah:

*So I pierced his garments with the deaf spear,*
*the noble man, against the spear-points, is not one in a state of ihram.*

He meant: "So I pierced him with the spear."

[Page 277 continues]

As for His words ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Great﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 74], it may be that it is of the type of ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise﴾ [al-Nasr: 3], meaning that the intent is to say words that contain glorification of God, and thus it is of the type of His words "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." It may also be that the *ba'* is extra (*za'idah*), in which case it is equivalent to His words ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1].

This *kinayah* is among the subtleties of speech, like the saying: "Doubt does not attach to its edges," and the verse of the poet:

*Her house spends the night safe from blame,*
*when other houses have been visited by reproach.*

A parallel to this in the matter of glorification is that the Qur'an may be recited by one who is not in a state of ablution, but according to the majority of jurists, only one who is in a state of ablution may touch the mushaf.

The mention of (*ism*) in His words ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ takes into account that what has been enumerated of God's affairs, His blessings, and His bounties cannot be encompassed by expression. So He expressed it with this intensification, since it is the furthest that language permits in expression, so that people may know that they owe God a gratitude that matches the greatness of His blessings upon them.

Invoking the Majesty through the title (*Rabb*), in construct with a pronoun of the addressee, who is the Prophet (ﷺ), indicates what the meaning of *Rabb* contains of sovereignty mingled with tenderness and nurturing; and what the idiom contains of honoring the one addressed; and that the Prophet (ﷺ) is the intermediary in the attainment of those goods for those who feared the station of their Lord, through what the Prophet (ﷺ) conveyed to them of guidance.

The majority of reciters read (*dhi al-jalal*) with a *ya'* in the genitive, as an adjective of *Rabbika* ("your Lord"), and it is written thus in copies other than the Syrian *mushaf*. Ibn 'Amir read it as (*dhu al-jalal*), as an adjective of (*ism*), as in His words ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman: 27]. Likewise, it is written thus in copies other than the *mushaf* of the people of Syria. The meaning is one under both considerations.

However, the consensus of the reciters on the nominative (*raf'*) of (*dhu al-jalal*), which occupies the position of ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27], and the difference in transmission regarding the genitive of ﴿dhi al-jalal﴾ here, suggests that the word (*wajh*, "face") is a stronger indicator of the essence than the word (*ism*, "name"), as you know, because it is possible that the meaning is the flowing of blessing

[Page 278]

upon the pronunciation of God's names, unlike His words ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27]. This is among the wisdoms of the revelation of the Qur'an in seven *ahruf* (the seven modes of recitation).

*Al-jalal* is greatness, and it encompasses the attributes of perfection that are befitting to Him, exalted is He. *Al-ikram* is bestowing blessing and good, and so it is a dignity worthy of praise and gratitude.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Surat al-Waqi'ah. This surah was named "al-Waqi'ah" by the naming of the Prophet (ﷺ).

At-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Abu Bakr said, "O Messenger of God, I have grayed." He said: "Hud, al-Waqi'ah, al-Mursalat, 'Amma yatasa'alun, and Idha al-shams kuwwirat have grayed me." At-Tirmidhi said: this is a *hasan gharib* hadith.

Ibn Wahb and al-Bayhaqi narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, with a weak chain, that he heard the Messenger of God say: "Whoever recites Surat al-Waqi'ah every night, poverty will never afflict him." It was likewise named in the era of the Companions. Ahmad narrated from Jabir ibn Samurah, who said: "The Messenger of God used to recite al-Waqi'ah and similar surahs in the dawn prayer."

Thus it is named in the *mushafs* and in the books of Sunnah, and no other name for it is known.

It is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: by the agreement of those among the exegetes whose opinion is considered. It was said that some verses of it are Medinan, meaning that they were revealed during a journey, but all of this is not established. [End of quotation.] Al-Qurtubi said, citing Qatadah and Ibn 'Abbas, that the exception of His words ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82] was revealed in Medina. Al-Kalbi said: except four verses: two were revealed during the Prophet's (ﷺ) journey to Mecca, and they are ﴿Is it this discourse that you disdain?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 81] and ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82]; and two were revealed during his journey to Medina, and they are ﴿A multitude of the former peoples﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 39] and ﴿And a multitude of the latter peoples﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 40]. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that it was revealed during the Battle of Tabuk.

[Page 280]

It is the forty-sixth surah in the order of revelation of the surahs according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat Ta-Ha and before Surat al-Shu'ara'.

The people of Medina, Mecca, and Syria counted its verses as ninety-nine, the people of Basra counted them as ninety-seven, and the people of Kufa counted them as ninety-six.

This surah comprehensively contains reminders. Masruq said: "Whoever wishes to know the news of the former and latter peoples, the news of the people of Paradise, the news of the people of Hellfire, the news of the people of this world, and the news of the people of the Hereafter, let him recite Surat al-Waqi'ah." [End of quotation.]

The reminder of the Day of Resurrection and affirming its occurrence.

Description of what is presented, and of this terrestrial world at the hour of the Resurrection.

Then the description of the people of Paradise and some of their bliss.

The description of the people of Hellfire, what they are in of punishment, and that this is due to their denial of the Resurrection. The affirmation of the gathering and recompense, and the argument for the possibility of the second creation through what God has originated of existents after they were not.

Argument through the evidences of God's power.

Argument through God's extraction of souls from bodies, while people are unwilling, and no one can prevent them from departing. This is based on the fact that He who is able to extract them without any opponent is able to return them whenever He wishes to cause them to die.

Affirmation that the Qur'an is sent down from God, that it is a blessing He bestowed upon them, yet they did not thank Him for it, and they denied what it contains.
